title: Follow a claim back to its source with Grok
summary: Check whether an announcement says what someone thinks it says.

intro.what: Grok is a helper that can answer questions. Some versions can search the web or X for public posts. Grok Bot is a separate way to give a helper a task.
intro.features: You can look for an original post, read a public policy or try a tool made for pictures, video or speech.
intro.exchange: Look up a public mail service notice. Compare the time in the post with the service’s own update.
intro.m365: Find the original announcement behind a public feature summary. Check its date.
intro.developer: Find the page that explains a tool your app uses. Save the link with your notes.

sections.title: Find out how far the claim goes
paragraphs: Imagine a post says a ferry now leaves at noon. Open Grok and ask it to find the operator’s original post. Ask for the date, route and sailing day. Open the link. One noon sailing on Saturday does not tell you when Monday’s ferry leaves. Check the official timetable too. An app you build needs search enabled to get fresh posts.

sections.title: Choose the kind of answer you need
paragraphs: The API model {{model.xai.grok.name}} accepts pictures and text and writes back in text. Its context window fits {{model.xai.grok.context}}. Try a picture of a short sign. Ask which word is hard to read. To make a clip or a new picture, look for {{model.xai.imagine.name}}. To build spoken chat, look for {{model.xai.voice.name}}. Use the Grok Bot quickstart to practice handing off a small job.

title: Search with Perplexity and read with Comet
summary: Ask for a source. Open it and check the sentence behind the answer.

intro.what: Perplexity helps you look up an answer. Comet is a browser with a helper beside the pages you open.
intro.features: Search can give you source links. Comet can help you read or compare tabs. Its permissions control what the assistant may see.
intro.exchange: Find the public help page for a mail command. Read its example before using it in a report.
intro.m365: Check a public release note for the date a feature starts. Distinguish it from the date of the post.
intro.developer: Compare two tools for making game sounds. Check the terms for saving a sound file.

sections.title: Check one answer
paragraphs: Ask Perplexity for the Saturday hours of a public museum of your choice. Open its source. Does the page actually list Saturday? Does it give hours for the date you picked? If it only links to the museum’s home page, ask for the calendar entry. For an older app, {{model.perplexity.sonar.name}} ended on {{model.perplexity.sonar.end}}. The developer guide explains the move to the Agent API.

sections.title: Compare two pages in Comet
paragraphs: Open two public sample booking pages. Ask Comet which deadline each gives for changing a booking. Request the date, time, time zone and source line. Read both pages. A general help page may describe a different ticket. Check which tabs you shared in Comet’s controls. Its iPad controls may sit in a different place from the desktop controls.

intro.what: Muse is Meta’s personal AI helper. You can give it a goal, leave it to work and then review the result.
intro.features: It can draft a plan, make a file, set up a later task or work with an app you connect. Its Library holds finished files.
intro.exchange: Draft a checklist for reviewing a pretend mailbox report. Tick off each check as you try it.
intro.m365: Make a plan from a pretend meeting note. Check each date against the note.
intro.developer: Use Muse to draft the rules for a card game. Play a round on paper to spot missing rules.

sections.title: Give it a tiny job
paragraphs: Open the Muse quickstart in this book. You can follow the example on paper if you cannot use the service. Give it this made-up note: “Game night. Bring cards and a pencil. Set up at six.” Ask for a short checklist. Does it include both items? Did it keep six as the setup time? Ask it to fix one missing detail.

sections.title: Check the result before sharing it
paragraphs: If Muse made a file, open Library and find its title. Open the file and read the actual words. A message saying “done” tells you to look for the result. It still needs a check. Later, try the illustrated lessons on reminders, linked apps and approvals. You can practice the checklist above without linking an inbox.

title: Meet Meta Muse
summary: Give a personal helper one small job and inspect what comes back.

title: Try a speech tool or run a model offline
summary: Learn the difference between downloading this book and downloading an AI that can answer new questions.

intro.what: Mistral Vibe can help with writing and code. A speech model works with sound. A local model runs on the computer you have in front of you.
intro.features: You can test a minute of audio, try a coding chat or download a model and a compatible app to use it.
intro.exchange: Use a local model on a small pretend mail report. Compare one answer with a row.
intro.m365: Try a short sample recording. Check which speaker gave the meeting time.
intro.developer: Use a small local model to sort five game items into groups. Test it again with the network off.

sections.title: Listen to one minute first
paragraphs: Mistral Vibe offers chat and coding sessions. The {{model.mistral.voxtral.name}} family includes tools for speech. Look up the languages and tasks the model supports. Make a pretend recording with two voices, a pause and a number. Ask for a transcript. Play back the number. Check which person said it. A smooth summary can hide a wrong word.

sections.title: Make a real offline test
paragraphs: Google offers downloadable models such as {{model.google.gemma.name}}. A model download holds the numbers an AI learned. You also need an app that can load that exact format. Check the memory it needs before downloading. Open the app once while online. Turn the network off, restart the app and ask a new question about a file saved on the device. A saved answer alone does not prove that a new question works.

title: What can a browser helper see?
summary: Use two small pages to learn which tabs you have shared.

intro.what: A browser is an app such as Chrome or Safari that opens websites. An extension is a tool added to a browser. Some browsers include their own AI helper.
intro.features: A helper can read a page you share or work inside a browser. Its access depends on the app, its settings and the device.
intro.exchange: Compare two public mail help pages. Check which page the helper actually quoted.
intro.m365: Ask a helper to explain one paragraph from a public meeting guide. Share that paragraph.
intro.developer: Open your app’s help page and test whether the helper can find the button named on it.
sources: Chrome Help · manage extension site access

sections.title: Share just what the job needs
paragraphs: If you need help with one sentence, copy it into chat. For a job across two tabs, open the browser helper and check which tabs it can read. In Chrome, go to Extensions and open the tool’s details. See whether you can limit access to selected sites or to one click. Read a draft before letting a helper press a button that sends it.
sources: Chrome Help · manage extension site access

sections.title: Try a two-page test
paragraphs: On a computer, open two public pages with different hours. Share one page and ask for both sets of hours. Check which page the answer actually cites. Share the second page and ask again. On iPad, use a supported app or browser. Choosing “Add to desktop” on a phone can queue the extension for your computer.
sources: Chrome Help · manage extension site access
